ideas.name: Arithmetic of remainders
ideas.statement: Sums and products mod m depend only on the remainders of the parts; a factor c can be cancelled when gcd(c, m) = 1.

ideas.name: Multiplication permutes residues mod a prime
ideas.statement: For a prime p and a not divisible by p, the residues of a, 2a, ..., (p-1)a are 1, ..., p-1 in some order.

ideas.name: Fermat's little theorem
ideas.statement: For a prime p and a not divisible by p, a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p).

ideas.name: Modular inverse
ideas.statement: Mod a prime p, every a not divisible by p has exactly one x with ax = 1, and x = a^(p-2).

ideas.name: The gcd survives subtraction
ideas.statement: gcd(a, b) = gcd(a - b, b): the pairs have the same common divisors.

ideas.name: Euclid's algorithm
ideas.statement: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b), and a mod b < a/2, so it finishes in O(log) steps.

ideas.name: Bézout's identity
ideas.statement: ax + by = c has integer solutions exactly when gcd(a, b) divides c.

ideas.name: Divisors from prime exponents
ideas.statement: If n is the product of p_i^e_i, its divisors correspond to independent choices of exponents: there are prod(e_i + 1) of them.

ideas.name: Harmonic sum over multiples
ideas.statement: Visiting every multiple of every i up to n costs n/1 + n/2 + ... + n/n = O(n log n).

ideas.name: A running gcd changes few times
ideas.statement: Each time a running gcd changes it at least halves, so it takes at most log2(a) different values.

ideas.name: Chinese remainder theorem
ideas.statement: For coprime m and n, the pair (x mod m, x mod n) determines x mod mn, and every pair occurs.

ideas.name: Parity invariant
ideas.statement: If every move changes a count by an even amount, its parity is fixed forever; a target of the other parity is unreachable.

ideas.name: Invariants modulo m
ideas.statement: A quantity that every move changes by a multiple of m keeps its remainder mod m; some are preserved exactly.

ideas.name: Monovariant
ideas.statement: A non-negative integer that strictly decreases with every move forces the process to stop, and bounds the number of moves.

ideas.name: Colouring argument
ideas.statement: Colour the cells so that every piece covers a fixed colour pattern; an unbalanced board cannot be covered.

ideas.name: Cycles of a permutation
ideas.statement: A permutation splits into disjoint cycles. Sorting it takes n minus (number of cycles) swaps, and applying it k times moves each element k mod (its cycle length) steps.

ideas.name: Parity of a permutation
ideas.statement: Every swap flips the parity of the number of inversions, so the parity of the number of swaps is determined.

ideas.name: Extremal principle
ideas.statement: Look at the smallest, largest, first or last object: its extremeness gives a property that others lack.

ideas.name: Canonical form
ideas.statement: To decide whether two objects count as the same, reduce each to one agreed representative: equal representatives exactly when the objects are the same. Grouping is then sorting or hashing the representatives.

ideas.name: Extend a small construction
ideas.statement: Solve n = 1, 2, 3 by hand and find the step that turns a solution for n into one for n + 1 or n + 2.

ideas.name: Necessary, then sufficient
ideas.statement: Find the obstruction that rules out some inputs, then construct an answer for every input that passes it.

ideas.name: Pigeonhole principle
ideas.statement: More objects than boxes forces two objects into one box.

ideas.name: Two equal prefix remainders
ideas.statement: Among n + 1 prefix sums two share a remainder mod n, so some block of consecutive elements sums to a multiple of n.

ideas.name: Contribution counting
ideas.statement: A sum over all objects of a sum over their parts equals a sum over parts of how many objects contain each.

ideas.name: Complement counting
ideas.statement: Count everything, then subtract what fails: often the failures are far easier to describe.

ideas.name: Stars and bars
ideas.statement: The number of ways to write n as an ordered sum of k non-negative integers is C(n + k - 1, k - 1).

ideas.name: Lattice paths and binomials
ideas.statement: Paths of r right steps and u up steps number C(r + u, r); many counts are such paths in disguise.

ideas.name: Inclusion-exclusion
ideas.statement: The size of a union is the alternating sum of the sizes of the intersections.

ideas.name: Linearity of expectation
ideas.statement: The expected value of a sum is the sum of the expected values, whether or not the parts are independent.

ideas.name: Exchange argument
ideas.statement: If swapping two adjacent out-of-order choices never makes the answer worse, the sorted order is optimal.

ideas.name: Greedy stays ahead
ideas.statement: Show by induction that after every step the greedy choice is at least as good as any other solution's.

ideas.name: Greedy with undo
ideas.statement: Take every option, and when a constraint breaks, undo the worst choice so far (a heap finds it).

ideas.name: Binary search on the answer
ideas.statement: If 'can it be done with x?' is false then true as x grows, the smallest workable x is found by halving.

ideas.name: Halving between a no and a yes
ideas.statement: Keep two points: one where the answer is no and one where it is yes. Test the middle and move the end that matches. The two stay a no and a yes, and after about $\log_2$(range) tests they are neighbours: that is the boundary.

ideas.name: Largest possible minimum
ideas.statement: To make the smallest of several things as large as possible, ask "can every one of them be at least $x$?", answer that with a greedy pass, and search for the last $x$ that says yes.

ideas.name: k-th value by counting
ideas.statement: The k-th smallest value is the least x for which at least k values are <= x.

ideas.name: Searching for an average
ideas.statement: "Is there a stretch with average at least $x$?" becomes "is there a stretch of $a_i - x$ with sum at least 0?", which prefix sums answer. Then search for the largest such $x$; for a real answer, halve a fixed number of times.

ideas.name: Prefix sums
ideas.statement: With P[i] = a[1] + ... + a[i], any block sum is P[r] - P[l - 1].

ideas.name: Blocks as pairs of prefixes
ideas.statement: Counting blocks with a given sum is counting pairs of prefix values with a given difference.

ideas.name: Difference array
ideas.statement: Adding v to a whole block is two point updates on the array of differences.

ideas.name: Two pointers
ideas.statement: If moving the left end right can only move the best right end right, both ends sweep once: O(n).

ideas.name: Prefix XOR
ideas.statement: The XOR of a block is the XOR of two prefix XORs, because x xor x = 0.

ideas.name: What a state must remember
ideas.statement: A state is a summary of the past that is enough to decide the future; two histories with the same summary can be merged.

ideas.name: Knapsack and the order of loops
ideas.statement: Looping capacity downward uses each item once; upward allows it again and again.

ideas.name: Subsets as states
ideas.statement: When order matters only through which items are used, the set of used items is the state: 2^n of them.

ideas.name: Intervals as states
ideas.statement: Solve every block [l, r] from shorter blocks by choosing the last operation or a split point.

ideas.name: Digit by digit
ideas.statement: Counting numbers up to N: build digits from the top, remembering only whether the prefix is still equal to N's.

ideas.name: Answers for every root
ideas.statement: Compute each subtree's answer, then push the answer of 'everything outside the subtree' down from the parent.

ideas.name: Configurations as a graph
ideas.statement: Make each configuration a vertex and each move an edge; fewest moves is a shortest path.

ideas.name: Run time backwards
ideas.statement: Deletions are hard, insertions are easy: process the operations in reverse and merge.

ideas.name: Two-colourable means no odd cycle
ideas.statement: A graph can be split into two sides with all edges across exactly when it has no cycle of odd length.

ideas.name: XOR undoes itself
ideas.statement: x xor x = 0 and XOR is associative and commutative, so anything XORed twice disappears.

ideas.name: Each bit on its own
ideas.statement: For AND, OR and XOR every bit position behaves independently; solve for one bit and add up 2^b times the count.

ideas.name: Subsets as bitmasks
ideas.statement: A subset of n items is an n-bit number; going through every subset of every subset costs 3^n.

ideas.name: Sum, XOR and AND
ideas.statement: a + b = (a xor b) + 2 (a and b): XOR adds without carries, AND is the carries.

ideas.name: Count one, multiply by the symmetry
ideas.statement: If shifting, rotating or relabelling turns every valid arrangement into another valid one, count the arrangements with one coordinate pinned and multiply by the number of ways to pin it.

ideas.name: A bound and a strategy that meet
ideas.statement: Show that no play can do better than some value, then show one way of playing that reaches it; the two together are the answer.

ideas.name: Pairs that cannot both survive
ideas.statement: Find pairs of objects of which exactly one can be taken whatever you do; the problem then splits into one small choice per pair.

ideas.name: Settle the far end first
ideas.statement: When pieces are brought to their places one at a time, choose the order of places so that a finished piece is never in the way of what remains. Then each piece is an ordinary shortest-route problem.

ideas.name: Fast exponentiation
ideas.statement: a^e needs only about 2 log2(e) multiplications: square repeatedly and multiply the powers picked out by the binary digits of e.

ideas.name: Sieve of smallest prime factors
ideas.statement: Marking the multiples of each prime up to n gives every number its smallest prime factor, so any number up to n factorises in O(log n).

ideas.name: Binomials modulo a prime
ideas.statement: With factorials and inverse factorials precomputed mod p, C(n, k) = n! * inv(k!) * inv((n-k)!) in O(1).

ideas.name: Disjoint set union
ideas.statement: Keep each group as a tree of parent pointers; merge the smaller tree under the larger and shorten paths as you walk them, and each operation is almost constant time.

ideas.name: Minimum spanning tree by sorted edges
ideas.statement: Take edges from cheapest to dearest, keeping an edge exactly when it joins two different groups; a swap argument shows nothing cheaper exists.

ideas.name: Topological order
ideas.statement: Repeatedly remove a vertex with no incoming edges; if you get stuck there is a cycle, otherwise the removal order respects every edge.

ideas.name: Shortest paths by settling the nearest
ideas.statement: With non-negative lengths, the unsettled vertex with the smallest tentative distance already has its true distance.

ideas.name: Fenwick tree
ideas.statement: Store sums of blocks whose lengths are the lowest set bit of the index; a prefix sum and a point update each touch O(log n) blocks.

ideas.name: Segment tree
ideas.statement: Store an answer for each of 2n - 1 halving blocks; any range splits into O(log n) of them and a point change touches O(log n).

ideas.name: Sparse table
ideas.statement: Precompute the answer for every block of length 2^k; when overlap is harmless (min, max, gcd) any range is two blocks.

ideas.name: Lowest common ancestor by doubling
ideas.statement: Store the 2^k-th ancestor of every vertex; lift the deeper vertex, then lift both together from the largest jump down.

ideas.name: Polynomial hashing
ideas.statement: Treat a string as a number in base b modulo p; the hash of any substring comes from two prefix hashes, so equal substrings can be compared in O(1).

ideas.name: Bridges
ideas.statement: An edge is a bridge exactly when it lies on no cycle. In a DFS tree, the tree edge down to v is a bridge exactly when no other edge leaves the subtree of v.

ideas.name: Many starting points at once
ideas.statement: To find the distance from every vertex to the nearest of several special vertices, start one breadth-first search with all of them at distance 0.

ideas.name: Winning and losing positions
ideas.statement: A position is losing if every move leads to a winning position, and winning if some move leads to a losing one; work backwards from the end and look for the pattern.

ideas.name: Games of fixed length
ideas.statement: If every way of playing takes the same number of moves, nobody has a real choice: the winner is decided by the parity of that number.

ideas.name: Copy the opponent
ideas.statement: If you can always answer a move with its mirror image, you never run out of moves before your opponent does.

ideas.name: Each edge splits the tree
ideas.statement: Removing an edge of a tree leaves parts of sizes s and n - s; exactly s(n - s) pairs of vertices have their path through that edge.

ideas.name: Nim and the XOR of the piles
ideas.statement: In Nim the player to move loses exactly when the XOR of the pile sizes is 0: from XOR 0 every move breaks it, and from any other value some move restores it.

ideas.name: Blocks and boundaries
ideas.statement: An operation on a binary string usually changes only the boundaries between blocks of equal characters, and by at most two: count blocks, not characters.

ideas.name: Inversions of a binary string
ideas.statement: The pairs (a 1, a later 0) measure how unsorted a binary string is; a swap of neighbours changes the count by exactly one.

ideas.name: Balance as a walk
ideas.statement: Score +1 and -1 for the two characters: equal counts are equal prefix values, and a correct bracket sequence is a walk that never goes below zero and ends at zero.

ideas.name: Parity of positions
ideas.statement: An operation that moves characters by two places keeps each character on positions of the same parity, so the counts on odd and on even positions are invariants.

ideas.name: Palindromes grow from centres
ideas.statement: A string of length n has 2n - 1 centres, and every palindromic substring is found by expanding from one of them; the first half of a palindrome determines the rest.

ideas.name: Rearranging into a palindrome
ideas.statement: Letters can be rearranged into a palindrome exactly when at most one letter occurs an odd number of times; for substrings, compare prefix masks of letter parities.

ideas.name: Palindromic subsequences
ideas.statement: The longest palindromic subsequence is the longest common subsequence of a string and its reverse; the fewest insertions to make a palindrome is the length minus it.

ideas.name: Palindromes and periods
ideas.statement: If a palindrome of length n has a palindromic prefix of length m, then n - m is a period of it; a string of length n has at most n different palindromic substrings.

ideas.name: Counting pairs by their gcd
ideas.statement: Pairs whose gcd is a multiple of g are simply pairs of multiples of g. Going from large g to small and subtracting the counts for 2g, 3g, ... leaves the pairs with gcd exactly g.

ideas.name: Floor division takes few values
ideas.statement: As i runs from 1 to n, the quotient n // i takes at most about 2 sqrt(n) different values, each on a block of consecutive i, so sums involving it can be done block by block.

ideas.name: Euler's totient
ideas.statement: phi(n) counts the numbers up to n that share no factor with n; it equals n times (1 - 1/p) over the primes p dividing n, and a^phi(n) = 1 mod n whenever a shares no factor with n.

ideas.name: Storing and walking a graph
ideas.statement: Keep, for every vertex, the list of its neighbours. A walk from a start vertex that marks vertices as it reaches them visits each vertex and each edge once, and gives distances, components, parents, and (processed in reverse) anything about subtrees.

ideas.name: Count with a table of what you have seen
ideas.statement: To count pairs with a relation between their two elements, go left to right and, for each element, look up how many earlier elements would complete a pair; then record the element.

ideas.name: Monotonic stack
ideas.statement: Sweeping once and discarding every element that a later, at-least-as-large element makes useless leaves a decreasing stack whose top is the nearest greater element; each element is pushed and popped once.

ideas.name: How far a minimum reaches
ideas.statement: An element is the minimum of exactly (i - L)(R - i) stretches, where L and R are its nearest smaller neighbours; summing value times that count handles every stretch at once.

ideas.name: Monotonic queue
ideas.statement: The candidates for the maximum of a sliding window form a decreasing queue: new values remove candidates from the back, expired positions leave from the front, and the front is the maximum.

ideas.name: Best partner so far
ideas.statement: To optimise over pairs $i < j$, sweep $j$ from left to right and keep only the best earlier element (sometimes two: the smallest and the largest). Each $j$ is then answered in one step, and when the roles flip you sweep from the other end.
